choices.correct_explanation:
A Gastrostomy tube is a medical device inserted into the stomach via the abdominal wall for providing long-term enteral nutrition to patients who cannot take food orally but have a functioning GI tract.

Table: Gastrostomy tube

Parameter

Details

Other names

PEG tube (Percutaneous Endoscopic Gastrostomy), Surgical G-tube, Balloon G-tube

Route

Percutaneous → Through anterior abdominal wall into stomach

Indications

Neurogenic dysphagia (stroke, Parkinson’s), head/neck cancer, esophageal stricture, long-term ventilated patients, anorexia, unconsciousness

Contraindications

Uncorrected coagulopathy, severe ascites, gastric varices, peritonitis

Insertion techniques

1. Surgical gastrostomy (open/laparoscopic) 2. Percutaneous Endoscopic Gastrostomy (PEG) – most common

Tube material

Medical-grade silicone or polyurethane – flexible, biocompatible, non-reactive

Securing mechanism

Internal bumper or balloon, and external fixation plate

Tube sizes

Typically 14 Fr to 24 Fr (measured in French units, where 1 Fr = 0.33 mm in diameter)

Length

Pediatric: ~15–20 cm; Adult: ~20–30 cm

Feeding methods

Bolus, intermittent gravity feeding, or continuous pump-based feeding

Type of feed

Isotonic, polymeric formulas unless otherwise indicated

Patency maintenance

Flush with 30–50 mL of sterile water before and after feeding

Common complications

Site infection, tube blockage, leakage, peritonitis, aspiration (rare), tube migration

Nursing responsibilities

Site care, tube rotation, monitoring for signs of infection or leakage, checking residual volume before feeding

 

Distractors:

Nasogastric Tube (Ryle’s Tube)

• Pap/Papanicolaou test is a screening test only. The presence of abnormal cells or a positive test requires further evaluation by colposcopy, cervical biopsy, or fractional curettage.

Screening Guidelines:

  • Time for initiation: 21 years, regardless of the age of first sexual intercourse.
  • Women aged 21-29 years: Every 3 years (earlier it was done annually).
  • Women who are aged 30-65 years: Pap test + HPV testing every 5 years.
  • Women should stop having cervical cancer screening after the age of 65 years. If suspicious PAP, screening till 75 years.
  • HIV+ women: Annual check-up until three consecutive negative tests followed by testing every 3 years for life.
  • HPV DNA testing in combination with PAP improves the sensitivity of screening.

Instrument

  • The given set of instruments are commonly used for the collection of pap smears. The given image includes Cusco’s bivalved self-retaining speculum, Koplin’s jar, smear slides, Ayer’s spatula, and endocervical brush.

Prerequisites:

  • Should be done prior to vaginal examination.
  • Lubricants should not be used.
  • The patient should not be menstruating during the pap test.
  • The ideal time is around ovulation.
  • The patient should not have had intercourse in the 24 hours prior to the test.

Procedure:

  • The patient is put in a dorsal position and the labia are separated.
  • Cusco’s self-retaining speculum is introduced/posterior vaginal wall retractor is used.
  • The squamocolumnar junction is identified and scraped with Ayre’s spatula.
  • Endocervix is scraped with a cytobrush.
  • Samples are spread separately on 2 different glass slides.
  • The slide is immediately fixed using 95% ethyl alcohol.
  • Stained with Pap stain or Short stain.

choices.correct_explanation:
• The image shows Depo-Provera (Medroxyprogesterone acetate 150 mg/mL), a long-acting injectable contraceptive.

Mechanism of Action:

Depo-Provera works mainly by:

  • Inhibiting the LH surge, which prevents ovulation (primary mechanism) Thickening cervical mucus, making it impermeable to sperm
  • Altering the endometrial lining, making it less receptive to implantation

The most crucial action is suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis, especially inhibiting LH, thereby blocking ovulation.

  • Inhibits FSH release and prevents ovulation
    • Partially true, but LH suppression is the dominant action for Depo-Provera.
    • FSH inhibition is more relevant to estrogen-containing contraceptives.
  • Creates mechanical barrier to sperm: Describes barrier methods like condoms or diaphragms, not hormonal injectables.
  • Prevents fertilized ovum implantation via copper toxicity: This refers to copper IUDs, not hormone-based injectables like Depo-Provera.

Summary: Depo-Provera is a progestin-only injectable contraceptive that primarily inhibits the LH surge, thereby suppressing ovulation. Hence, Option B is correct.

choices.title: Prague maneuver
choices.correct_explanation:
• Prague’s maneuver is shown in the image. It is used in breech presentations to deliver the ‘after coming head’ when the back of the fetus fails to rotate to the symphysis.

Technique:

  • Grasp the shoulders of the baby from below with two fingers of one hand.
  • Draw the feet up and over the maternal abdomen with the other hand.

Other options:

McRoberts Maneuver

  • The first maneuver to be used in shoulder dystocia since it is the most successful intervention.
  • It involves flexing and abducting the mother’s hips to place her thighs on her belly.
  • The technique causes the symphysis pubis to rotate in the direction of the mother’s head, the sacrum to straighten in relation to the lumbar vertebrae, and the angle of the pelvic inclination to diminish.
  • Pelvic rotation has the tendency to release the impinged anterior shoulder, despite the fact that this does not enhance pelvic dimensions. It is possible to utilize suprapubic pressure concurrently.
  • The nerve most frequently hurt by this maneuver is the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh.

Ritgen Maneuver

  • Ritgen maneuver is done in delivery of head in normal labor. (Best way to prevent perineal tear).
  • Promoting flexion of fetal head with left hand and supporting perineum with right hand.
  • This maneuver allows controlled delivery of the head.

Modified Mauriceau-Smellie-Veit Technique

  • It is used in the delivery of after coming head in case of breech presentation.

Figure: Modified Mauriceau-Smellie-Veit technique

  • Technique: Malar flexion and shoulder traction
    • Baby placed on supine left forearm with arms hanging by the side.
    • Middle and index finger of left hand placed over baby’s malar bones to maintain flexion of head.
    • Pronated right hand, little and ring finger over baby’s right shoulder, middle finger over suboccipital region and index finger is placed on the left shoulder.
    • Traction is exerted in downward and backward direction and then in upward and forward direction once ape of neck is visible.

choices.title: Catastrophizing
choices.correct_explanation:
Catastrophizing is a type of cognitive distortion where a person:

  • Expects the worst possible outcome from a situation.
  • Blows minor issues out of proportion, imagining them as disastors.

 In this case:

  • Karamveer made a small mistake (minor issue).
  • But he believes he will be fired (extreme outcome).
  • Even though there's no actual indication — this is classic catastrophizing. 

Option clarification:

  • Personalization: Blaming oneself for events not under one's control ("It rained because I planned a picnic").
  • Filtering: Focusing only on the negative aspects while ignoring positives ("I messed up one line in a great presentation").
  • Emotional reasoning: Believing something is true because you feel it, regardless of evidence ("I feel useless, so I must be").

·         Electroconvulsive Therapy (ECT) involves administering a brief electrical stimulus to the brain under general anesthesia. Due to the anesthesia and muscle relaxants used, the risk of aspiration is significant if the patient has a full stomach.

·         Priority nursing action:

o    Ensuring NPO status (nothing by mouth) for at least 6–8 hours before the procedure is the highest priority, to prevent aspiration during anesthesia.

·        Option A. Remove all jewelry — Important, but not the highest priority. This prevents burns or interference, but doesn’t impact immediate safety like NPO status does.

choices.title: Discontinue risperidone and observe the patient without medication
Switch to a benzodiazepine to manage delusions
Start CBT only
choices.correct_explanation:
In the nursing management context, especially at a moderate level, non-pharmacological interventions like Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) become important once acute symptoms are partially controlled.

In this case:

  • The patient is already on risperidone and showing significant improvement, which means pharmacological treatment is effective to some extent.
  • Persecutory delusions are persistent, which is common in schizophrenia even with medication.
  • The role of nursing at this point includes:
    • Supporting psychosocial interventions
    • Reinforcing adherence
    • Initiating or supporting CBT, which helps the patient reframe distorted thoughts and reduce delusional intensity over time.

 

Thus, starting CBT aligns with a moderate-level nursing management plan, targeting residual symptoms and functional improvement.

 

Incorrect Options:

Start Risperidone syrup

  • This might be useful if non-compliance or swallowing difficulty was the issue.
  • But here, the patient is already improving on Risperidone, so there's no indication of administration issues.
  • Starting syrup offers no additional benefit if tablets are being taken regularly.

Discontinue risperidone and observe the patient without medication

  • Unsafe and inappropriate in a patient with persistent psychotic symptoms.
  • Discontinuation can lead to relapse or worsening of schizophrenia.

Switch to a benzodiazepine to manage delusions

  • Benzodiazepines are not used to treat delusions.
  • They are reserved for acute agitation or anxiety, not as long-term or core management for schizophrenia.

 Summary: Since the patient is already partially responding to medication, and the delusions persist, the nursing-level next step is to initiate CBT — making Option D the most appropriate answer in this scenario.

• The defect shown in the image is known as anencephaly which is a neural tube defect.
  • The neural tube consists of two pores:
    • Anterior pore (cranial neuropore): Closes by the 25th day   
    • Posterior pole (caudal neuropore): Closes by 28th day)
  • Anencephaly is a type of neural tube defect in which the brainand skull fail to develop properly, resulting in the absence of major portions of the brain and skull.  
  • Often diagnosed prenatally through ultrasound or other imaging tests.
  • Infants born with anencephaly are typically stillborn or die shortly after birth, as the condition is incompatible with life. 

 Other Options:

 Option A: 

  • A type of neural tube defect that involves a protrusion of the spinal cord and its covering (meninges) through an opening in the back.
  • It can cause nerve damage, paralysis, and other complications, depending on the severity and location of the defect.
  • It is often diagnosed prenatally through ultrasound or other imaging tests.

 Option B:  

  • A condition characterized by the build-up of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) in the brain, leading to increased pressure and swelling.

• Low height for age, or shunting, indicates chronic malnutrition not as acute malnutrition. This is the best indicator of long-term nutritional status in the pediatric population.
  • Low weight for the age indicates acute or chronic malnutrition. It does not differentiate between wasting and stunting. Hence it has limited clinical significance.

Severe acute malnutrition (SAM) in children of ages 6 to 59 months is defined by WHO as any of the following is found:

  • Weight-for-length (or height) below -3 SD of the WHO Child Growth Standards.
  • Presence of bipedal edema.
  • Mid-upper arm circumference <11.5 cm.

Once the child is diagnosed with severe acute malnutrition, the doctor must assess for severe edema (+++); low appetite (failed appetite test); medical complications (severe anemia, pneumonia, diarrhea, dehydration, cerebral palsy, tuberculosis, HIV, heart disease, etc.) and one or more danger signs as per IMNCI.    

If any of the complications are present, the child is diagnosed with complicated SAM and is managed in the facility. 

If the above-mentioned signs are absent, the child is diagnosed with uncomplicated SAM and supervised management is given at home.   

Treatment: The general treatment involves 10 steps in 2 phases:

Phases:

Initial stabilization phase: (mnemonic: SHIELDED- Sugar deficiency (hypoglycemia), hypothermia, infection, electrolyte imbalance, dehydration, deficiency of nutrients)  

  • Focuses on restoring homeostasis and treating medical conditions.
  • 2-7 days of inpatient treatment.

Rehabilitation phase:   

  • Focuses on rebuilding wasted tissues.
  • Takes several weeks.

Steps:  

  • Treat hypoglycemia (Blood glucose level<54 mg/dl): If symptomatic, give 10% Dextrose IV 5 ml/kg; feeding should be initiated with starter F-75 (Formula with 75 kcal/100 ml of feed).
  • Treat hypothermia (axillary <35°C or 95°F: Skin-to-skin contact with care ("kangaroo technique") or dress in warmer clothes, cover head, wrap in a warmed blanket, and provide indirect heat.
  • Treat dehydration: Hydrate with ReSoMal - Rehydration solution for malnutrition (45 mmol Na/L). It is a low-sodium rehydration solution for malnutrition.
  • Correct electrolyte imbalance: There is a deficit of potassium and magnesium and excess sodium. Give extra potassium (4 mmol/kg/day) and magnesium (0.6 mmol/kg/day) for at least 2 weeks.
  • Treat infection: Starting on the first day, give broad-spectrum antibiotics to all children.
  • Correct micronutrient deficiencies:
    • Do not give iron in the stabilization phase, because excess iron leads to free radical injury. Give iron 3 mg/kg/day once the child starts gaining weight after the stabilization phase.
    • Give vitamin A on day 1. Repeat on day 2 and day 14 if there is presence of xerophthalmia.
    • Folic acid 1 mg (5 mg on day 1)
    • Zinc (2 mg/kg/day)
    • Copper (0.3 mg/kg/day)
  • Start cautious feeding: Give 8 to 12 small feeds of F75 to provide 130 mL/kg/day, 100 kcal/kg/day, and 1 to 1.5 g protein/kg/day.
  • Rehabilitation: The indications of entry to this phase are reduced/minimal edema and the return of appetite.
    • Beginning of feeding.
    • After 3 days, the transition to energy-dense feeding.
    • Stimulation of emotional and sensorial development.
    • Transfer to home-based diet.

Corticosteroid therapy is a cornerstone in the management of nephrotic syndrome to reduce proteinuria and induce remission. However, corticosteroids have several important side effects that require close monitoring, the side effects are:

  • Hyperglycemia (increased blood glucose levels): Corticosteroids increase gluconeogenesis and decrease peripheral glucose utilization, which can lead to elevated blood sugar levels, even in non-diabetic patients.
  • Immunosuppression: Corticosteroids suppress the immune system, increasing the risk of infections, which can be severe and sometimes masked due to the blunting of inflammatory responses.

Thus, monitoring blood glucose levels and signs of infection (like fever, lethargy, or localized infections) is crucial when a child is on corticosteroid therapy.

Incorrect Options:

  • Option-A. Vitamin D and calcium deficiency: Long-term corticosteroid use can lead to bone demineralization, resulting in osteoporosis and deficiencies in calcium and vitamin D metabolism. However, this is more of a chronic concern and not an immediate priority for close monitoring in the initial or short-term phase of corticosteroid therapy, especially during an acute nephrotic syndrome episode.
  • Option-C. Signs of dehydration and electrolyte imbalance: Nephrotic syndrome typically presents with edema due to hypoalbuminemia and fluid retention, not dehydration. Electrolyte imbalances are not a primary concern unless diuretics are being used or there are other complicating factors like acute kidney injury. Thus, while maintaining fluid balance is important, close monitoring for dehydration is less critical in a child solely on corticosteroids.
  • Option-D. Blood pressure and urinary tract obstruction: While blood pressure monitoring is important in renal disorders (especially in cases with associated hypertension or fluid overload), urinary tract obstruction is not a typical feature of nephrotic syndrome.
    Also, corticosteroids themselves are not directly linked to cause urinary tract obstruction. Therefore, this option is less relevant to corticosteroid therapy in nephrotic syndrome.

choices.correct_explanation:
Point D is the Sampling Port

  • This is the designated site for sterile urine collection in patients with indwelling urinary catheters.
  • It is designed specifically for diagnostic sampling — either with a needleless syringe or a sterile needle, after proper disinfection (usually with 70% isopropyl alcohol or chlorhexidine).
  • It is equipped with a self-sealing membrane meant for needleless syringe aspiration or can be accessed via a sterile needle.
  • The sample obtained from this site reflects freshly voided urine directly from the bladder, minimizing the risk of contamination.

Scientific support:

  • According to the CDC Guidelines for Prevention of CAUTI (2023 update) and Infection Control Practices for Indwelling Catheters, urine samples must be collected from the sampling port using aseptic technique.
  • A study published in the American Journal of Infection Control (AJIC, 2022) reports a significant increase in false-positive cultures and antibiotic misuse when urine is collected from inappropriate sites like the drainage bag or tubing.
  • The Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) also strongly recommends avoiding culture collection from the drainage bag, as it leads to colonization-based results, not infection.

Note: Currently, it is not practiced to collect urine samples for culture directly from the catheter tubing or drainage bag. Instead, a separate, sterile sampling port is used specifically for this purpose in all standard hospital protocols.

Distractors:

Option 1 – Point A:

  • This is the proximal end of the catheter, connected to the drainage tubing.
  • Opening or disconnecting this site breaks the closed urinary drainage system, increasing risk of nosocomial infections, especially CAUTI.
  • Urine collected from here is not sterile due to external exposure and backflow risk.  

Option 2 – Point B:   

  • This is the balloon inflation port, used to inflate the retention balloon inside the bladder.
  • It is filled with sterile water (typically 10 mL) via a Luer-lock syringe to keep the catheter in place.
  • Attempting to aspirate urine from this port is both anatomically and clinically incorrect.
  • Tampering with this port could rupture or deflate the balloon, risking catheter dislodgement.

Option 3 – Point C:

  • This section is closer to the drainage bag.
  • Urine collected here is pooled and stagnant, leading to bacterial colonization and biofilm formation.
  • It does not represent the current state of the bladder's contents, leading to inaccurate culture reports.

Key points for nursing practice:

  • Always use the sampling port (Point D) for urine specimen collection.
  • Clean the port thoroughly before aspiration.
  • Use a sterile syringe/container.
  • Do not collect from the drainage bag, catheter tubing, or inflation port.
  • Maintain the integrity of the closed catheter system to reduce CAUTI risk.

choices.title: Increased intracranial pressure (ICP)
choices.correct_explanation:
Clinical background:

  • Lumbar puncture (LP) is a common diagnostic and therapeutic procedure involving the insertion of a needle into the subarachnoid space of the lumbar spine (typically between L3-L4 or L4-L5 vertebrae).
  • It allows CSF sampling, measurement of opening pressure, and administration of intrathecal medications.

Raised intracranial pressure (ICP):

  • Increased ICP refers to elevated pressure within the skull, often due to conditions such as intracranial tumors, cerebral edema, abscess, or hydrocephalus.
  • The Monro-Kellie Doctrine explains that the cranial compartment is incompressible, and an increase in one component (brain tissue, blood, or CSF) must be compensated by a decrease in another to maintain normal ICP.

Why LP is dangerous in raised ICP?   

  • Performing an LP suddenly reduces spinal CSF pressure.
  • This creates a pressure gradient between the intracranial and spinal compartments, especially in cases of mass lesions or cerebral edema.
  • The sudden change can pull the brainstem downward, leading to:
    • Tonsillar herniation through the foramen magnum.
    • Brainstem compression → respiratory arrest → death.
  • Brain herniation is a medical emergency with a high fatality rate.

Nursing points:

  • Absolute contraindication: Suspected or known raised ICP with focal neurologic signs, papilledema, or altered mental status.
  • Action: Perform neuroimaging (CT/MRI) before LP to rule out any mass effect.
  • Monitor signs of ICP: Bradycardia, hypertension, irregular respirations (Cushing's triad), headache, nausea, vomiting, blurred vision.
  • Always prioritize airway and ICP management before diagnostic LP.

Distractors:

Acute Bacterial Meningitis

  • LP is indicated, not contraindicated.
  • Rationale: CSF analysis is essential for diagnosis.
    • Elevated WBC count (neutrophils), low glucose, high protein.
    • CSF Gram stain and culture identify causative organisms.
  • If meningitis is suspected and LP is delayed due to possible raised ICP, start empirical antibiotics immediately.
  • Precaution: Do CT brain first only if focal neurologic signs or signs of raised ICP are present.

Multiple Sclerosis (MS) 

  • LP is indicated, especially when MRI is inconclusive.
  • CSF findings:
    • Oligoclonal bands (seen in >95% of MS cases).
    • Mildly elevated protein and lymphocytic pleocytosis.

  • Nursing tip: LP is safe in MS as ICP is typically not elevated.

Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (SAH)

  • LP is used for diagnosis, particularly when CT brain is negative but clinical suspicion is high.  
  • CSF findings:
    • Xanthochromia (yellow tint from RBC breakdown after 12 hours).
    • Persistent RBC count across all CSF collection tubes.
  • Contraindicated only if signs of raised ICP or obstructive hydrocephalus exist without imaging.
  • Best practice: CT head first. If CT is normal and SAH still suspected, perform LP after ruling out raised ICP.

choices.title: Hook technique
choices.correct_explanation:
Hook Technique

Parameter

Details

Definition

A BVM mask-holding technique where the provider uses one hand to form a "hook" with the thumb placed on the mask and the other four fingers wrapped under the mandible.

Grip description

Thumb on the top of the mask → Index, middle, ring, and little fingers positioned under the mandible (jawline), lifting the jaw upward.

Indications

Used for one-person BVM ventilation when a tight seal is difficult, or the provider has a large hand span.

Mechanism

Facilitates jaw thrust while maintaining a tight seal around the nose and mouth. Particularly useful in patients with facial hair, edentulism, or obesity.

Clinical consideration

Ensures airway patency by preventing tongue obstruction and leakage of oxygen. Helpful during CPR and emergency resuscitation when airway maintenance is critical.

Distractors

CE Technique

  • Incorrect terminology: There is no standardized technique officially called “CE” technique.
  • Confusion with E-C Clamp: Sometimes informally used to refer to the "E-C clamp" (see below), but not recognized as a distinct or separate method.
  • Always use standardized nomenclature (like “E-C clamp” or “Hook” or “Thenar Eminence” technique) to avoid clinical confusion.

E-C Clamp Technique

  • Commonly taught one-hand technique (Valid technique but not the one shown in the image).
  • Hand formation:
    • "E" = three fingers (middle, ring, and little) lift the mandible (jaw thrust).
    • "C" = thumb and index finger form a “C” shape to hold the mask down.
  • Limitation: Requires skill and practice to avoid air leak and ensure chest rise.
  • Most effective in non-obese adults with normal facial anatomy, and commonly taught in BLS/ACLS protocols.

Figure: E-C Clamp Technique

Two-Hand Thenar Eminence Technique

  • Used in two-rescuer CPR: One rescuer holds the mask with both hands using the thenar eminences (base of thumbs) on the mask, while another compresses the bag.
  • Technique:
    • Both thumbs press the mask down.
    • Fingers under mandible lift the jaw.
  • High seal efficiency: Provides superior mask seal and optimal tidal volume, especially in emergency or difficult airway cases.
  • Limitation: Requires two providers, not feasible in solo CPR.

Figure: Two-Hand Thenar Eminence Technique

BVM Techniques

Technique

Key Features

Hook technique

choices.title: Oxygen reservoir bag
choices.correct_explanation:
Bag-Valve-Mask (AMBU Bag):

The AMBU bag, also known as a Bag-Valve-Mask (BVM), is a hand-held device commonly used to provide positive pressure ventilation to patients who are apneic, hypoventilating, or undergoing cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR). It is a crucial tool in airway management and emergency life support settings, both in hospital and prehospital care.

Main components of the AMBU Bag:

1. Self-Inflating Bag  

  • Function: This is the core part of the AMBU bag that is manually compressed by the healthcare provider to push air or oxygen into the patient's lungs.         
  • Mechanism: It automatically re-inflates after each compression using a one-way valve system that draws in ambient air or oxygen.
  • Material: Typically made of medical-grade silicone or PVC and is collapsible.      
  • Clinical note: Allows ventilation even without an oxygen source (delivering ~21% FiO₂) but is more effective when connected to supplemental oxygen.

2. Oxygen Inlet Port 

  • Function: The port through which oxygen tubing connects to the bag from an external oxygen supply (e.g., wall outlet or portable cylinder).
  • Clinical note: Oxygen flow rate should be set to 10–15 liters per minute to ensure adequate reservoir bag inflation and high FiO₂ delivery.

3. Oxygen Reservoir Bag  

  • Function: This is an attachment that holds a reserve of pure oxygen, allowing for delivery of up to 90–100% FiO₂ during ventilation.
  • Working principle: When the self-inflating bag is squeezed, it draws oxygen from the reservoir rather than room air, provided the flow rate is adequate.
  • Clinical importance: Essential for critically ill or hypoxic patients needing high-concentration oxygen. 

4. Non-rebreathing valve (One-way Valve):

  • Function: Prevents exhaled air from re-entering the self-inflating bag or oxygen reservoir.
  • Mechanism: Ensures unidirectional airflow: Air flows to the patient on compression, and exhaled air is released to the atmosphere via an exhalation port.
  • Clinical note: Critical for maintaining high FiO₂ and preventing re-inhalation of carbon dioxide. 

5. Face Mask Connector

  • Function: Connects the bag-valve assembly to a face mask, endotracheal tube (ETT), or laryngeal mask airway (LMA).
  • Standard size: Typically 15 mm or 22 mm diameter, fitting standard airway devices.                 
  • Clinical note: A proper seal with the face mask is crucial to prevent air leaks and ensure effective ventilation.  

6. Face Mask 

  • Function: Delivers the ventilated air or oxygen directly to the patient’s mouth and nose. 
  • Design: Transparent, dome-shaped, often cushioned to ensure a good seal.
  • Clinical Tip: Use the "C-E" hand position to hold the mask and maintain airway patency using head-tilt/chin-lift.

Now referring back to the image – Labeled Part ‘A’

If the labeled part ‘A’ in the image is the soft, collapsible bag attached at the distal end of the AMBU bag opposite the face mask, then: Correct identification: (c) Oxygen Reservoir Bag

Rationale for the correct answer:

  • As described above, this component serves to store 100% oxygen from the oxygen supply and supplements the air being delivered through the self-inflating bag.
  • It is not self-inflating, has no valves, and has no direct patient interface, but its role is vital in improving oxygen delivery.
  • It must be fully inflated before use; a collapsed or poorly inflated reservoir indicates inadequate oxygen flow.

Part 'B' – PEEP Valve

  • Function: The PEEP (Positive End-Expiratory Pressure) valve maintains a small amount of pressure in the lungs at the end of expiration to help keep the alveoli open, preventing atelectasis and improving oxygenation.
  • Clinical importance:
    • This is crucial for patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), pneumonia, or those who require prolonged ventilation.
    • By preventing alveolar collapse, it enhances gas exchange, reduces the work of breathing, and improves oxygenation.
    • The PEEP valve helps prevent complications of ventilation such as hypoxemia and barotrauma.

Part 'C' – Pop-Off Valve

  • Function: The Pop-off valve is a safety feature designed to release air when the pressure in the system reaches a predetermined threshold, preventing excessive pressure from being applied to the patient’s lungs.
  • Clinical importance:
    • The pop-off valve ensures that the patient is not exposed to dangerously high pressures that could cause lung injury, such as barotrauma or pneumothorax.
    • It acts as a pressure-relief mechanism to maintain a safe ventilation pressure during manual ventilation.
    • It is especially important when ventilating patients who may have fragile or compromised lungs.

Distractors:

  • Self-inflating bag – Central compression component, not attached like the labeled part.
  • Oxygen inlet port – Small tubing connection point; not the bag shown in the image.
  • Face mask connector – Located at the patient-end, connects directly to face mask or airway; not the part labeled.

Clinical integration and related concepts:

  • Used in basic and advanced life support protocols.
  • Essential in managing respiratory failure, cardiac arrest, perioperative anesthesia, and emergency transport.
  • AMBU bags vary in volume (infant, pediatric, adult sizes) to avoid barotrauma.
  • Proper technique, including head positioning and bag compression rate (10–12 breaths/min in adults), is critical to avoid gastric insufflation or hypoventilation.

choices.correct_explanation:
Central Venous Pressure (CVP) reflects the pressure in the thoracic vena cava near the right atrium, essentially indicating right atrial pressure.

CVP is influenced by two main factors:

  1. Venous return (preload) → The amount of blood flowing back to the right atrium.
  2. Right ventricular function → The ability of the right ventricle to pump blood forward into the pulmonary circulation.

Thus, CVP represents a balance between:

  • The volume of blood entering the right heart.
  • The ability of the right heart to eject that blood.

If venous return increases (e.g., fluid overload) or right ventricular dysfunction occurs (e.g., right heart failure), CVP increases.

  • Option (a): Left ventricular contractility primarily affects systemic circulation, not CVP directly.
  • Option (b): Pulmonary vascular resistance affects right ventricular afterload, but not the primary determinant of CVP.
  • Option (d): Systemic arterial pressure is unrelated to CVP.

Therefore, the correct answer is (c): Volume of blood returning to the right atrium and the ability of the right ventricle to pump it forward.

  • Symptoms: Sudden severe abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, uterine tenderness

  • Key features:
    • Sudden, painful bleeding (may be concealed)
    • Rigid, tender uterus
    • Fetal distress or absence of fetal heart sounds in severe cases

    • Loss of fetal station, cessation of contractions
    • Palpable fetal parts per abdomen
    • Maternal shock often present

  • Fetal heart tones disappear suddenly after ROM
  • Very rare and not associated with uterine rigidity or tenderness

➡ This case shows pain, rigid uterus, and hypertension, which are not features of vasa previa.

The classic triad of:

  • Painful third-trimester bleeding
  • Tense, tender uterus
  • History of hypertension

Strongly indicates abruptio placentae. Hence, the correct answer is: C. Abruptio placentae.

choices.correct_explanation:
Arterial Blood Gas (ABG) and Venous Blood Gas (VBG) are both used to assess acid-base status, but there are key differences in the values they provide, especially for oxygenation.

  • pO₂ (Partial Pressure of Oxygen) is significantly higher in arterial blood because it reflects oxygen that has just been picked up from the lungs.
  • Venous blood reflects deoxygenated blood returning from tissues, hence has much lower pO₂.
  • Therefore, the most pronounced and clinically significant difference between ABG and VBG is the oxygenation parameter (pO₂).

Incorrect Options:

  • ABG and VBG show different hemoglobin (Hb) levels - Incorrect: Hemoglobin levels are measured from whole blood, and there is no significant difference between arterial and venous samples regarding Hb concentration.
  • ABG and VBG show identical values for all parameters - Incorrect: While some parameters (like pH, pCO₂, and bicarbonate) are comparable, they are not identical, and pO₂ values are markedly different.
  • ABG and VBG show significantly different potassium levels - Incorrect: Potassium levels in ABG and VBG are usually very similar and clinically interchangeable, unless there is hemolysis or sampling error.

Summary: While ABG and VBG can be used to assess acid-base and ventilation status interchangeably in many cases, pO₂ differs markedly, making Option C the correct and most clinically relevant choice.

The lethal triad is a life-threatening condition in trauma patients, particularly those with severe hemorrhagic shock, and consists of three interrelated physiological states:

  • Hypothermia: A drop in core body temperature (below 35°C or 95°F), often due to blood loss, exposure, or inadequate resuscitation.
  • Acidosis: Metabolic acidosis resulting from hypoperfusion and tissue hypoxia, leading to lactic acid buildup (pH < 7.2). 
  • Coagulopathy: Impaired blood clotting due to dilution of clotting factors, consumption during bleeding, or hypothermia/acidosis effects on the coagulation cascade.      

This triad creates a vicious cycle: hypothermia worsens coagulopathy, acidosis exacerbates both hypothermia and coagulopathy, and the resulting coagulopathy increases bleeding, further aggravating the other two conditions. It is a critical indicator of mortality in trauma and requires aggressive management (e.g., warming, correction of pH, and blood product transfusion).

It is not preferred in RSI due to its pharmacokinetic profile, which does not align with the need for rapid induction and quick recovery in an emergency setting. It is more commonly used for seizure control or procedural sedation outside of RSI.

Understanding Rapid Sequence Intubation (RSI):

  • RSI is a technique used to quickly secure the airway in emergency situations (e.g., trauma, respiratory failure) while minimizing the risk of aspiration. It involves:  
    • Induction agents: To render the patient unconscious (e.g., Propofol, Midazolam). 
    • Neuromuscular blocking agents (NMBAs): To paralyze muscles and facilitate intubation (e.g., succinylcholine).

Propofol:

  • A short-acting sedative-hypnotic used as an induction agent in RSI. It provides rapid onset (within 30–60 seconds) and is commonly used to induce unconsciousness. Dose is typically 1–2.5 mg/kg IV.
  • Typically used in RSI.

Midazolam:  

  • A benzodiazepine with sedative properties, used as an induction agent in RSI, especially in hemodynamically stable patients or when Propofol is contraindicated (e.g., hypotension). It has a slightly slower onset than Propofol but is still acceptable. Dose is typically 0.1–0.3 mg/kg IV.
  • Typically used in RSI.

Succinylcholine:

  • A depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent with a rapid onset (30–60 seconds) and short duration (5–10 minutes), making it a standard choice for muscle paralysis during RSI. Dose is typically 1–1.5 mg/kg IV.
  • Typically used in RSI.

choices.title: Calcium gluconate
choices.correct_explanation:
In severe hyperkalemia (elevated potassium levels, typically >6.5 mEq/L or with ECG changes), stabilizing the cardiac membrane is a critical initial step to prevent life-threatening arrhythmias. Calcium gluconate is administered as an IV bolus for this purpose. It works by reducing the excitability of the cardiac muscle by counteracting the effects of hyperkalemia on the cell membrane, particularly by stabilizing the cardiac action potential. This effect is immediate but temporary, lasting about 30–60 minutes, and it does not lower potassium levels—it only protects the heart.

In severe hyperkalemia, the most immediate concern is cardiac membrane instability, which can lead to life-threatening arrhythmias.

  • Calcium gluconate (or calcium chloride) is administered as an IV bolus to:
    • Stabilize the cardiac membrane
    • Reduce the excitability of myocardial cells
    • It does not lower serum potassium but buys time for other interventions to work.
  • Sodium bicarbonate: This is used to shift potassium into cells in cases of acidosis-associated hyperkalemia, but it is not a first-line agent for membrane stabilization. It is typically given as an IV infusion, not a bolus for this purpose.
  • Insulin with dextrose: This combination shifts potassium into cells by enhancing sodium-potassium ATPase activity, lowering serum potassium levels. It is a treatment for hyperkalemia but not for immediate cardiac membrane stabilization.
  • Salbutamol: This beta-2 agonist can also shift potassium into cells, but it is administered via inhalation or IV infusion, not as a bolus, and is not used for membrane stabilization.

Mnemonic for Hyperkalemia Emergency Management:

CBIGKD

  • C – Calcium gluconate (membrane stabilizer)
  • B – Beta-agonist (Salbutamol)
  • I – Insulin
  • G – Glucose (Dextrose)

choices.correct_explanation:
The Modified Early Warning Score (MEWS) is a tool used to assess a patient’s risk of clinical deterioration based on vital signs (heart rate, respiratory rate, systolic blood pressure, temperature, and level of consciousness).

  • A MEWS score of 7 indicates a high-risk patient who may be clinically unstable or rapidly deteriorating.
  • It warrants urgent medical review and intervention to prevent further decline or cardiac arrest. 
  • Often, it prompts activation of a rapid response team or transfer to a higher level of care such as HDU/ICU.

Incorrect options:  

Stable; routine monitoring:

  • This corresponds to a MEWS score of 0–2.
  • The patient is stable and does not require escalated care.
  • A score of 7 is well above this range, so this is incorrect.

Mild deterioration; reassess within 12 hours:

  • Applies to a MEWS score of 3–4.
  • Suggests closer observation or moderate concern
  • A score of 7 indicates a more critical situation than just mild deterioration.

Critical condition; immediate intensive care required:

  • Usually refers to MEWS > 8 or a rapidly rising score.
  • Though a MEWS of 7 is serious, it often prompts urgent intervention before ICU transfer, not automatic ICU admission.
  • Hence, "urgent intervention" is a more precise match than "immediate intensive care."

Summary: A MEWS score of 7 reflects significant clinical deterioration, requiring immediate evaluation and possibly life-saving interventions, but not necessarily ICU admission at that moment — making Option C the most appropriate response.

choices.title: Supraventricular Tachycardia (SVT)
choices.correct_explanation:
ECG Interpretation:

  • The ECG shows a narrow QRS complex tachycardia (QRS duration <120 ms)
  • The rate is very fast — typically 150–250 bpm
  • P waves are either absent or retrograde, and difficult to distinguish
  • There is no beat-to-beat variability, indicating a regular rhythm

These features are characteristic of Paroxysmal Supraventricular Tachycardia (PSVT), a form of SVT.

Incorrect Options:

Atrial Fibrillation

  • Atrial fibrillation shows:

    • Irregularly irregular rhythm
    • No distinct P waves
    • Chaotic baseline
  • In this ECG, the rhythm is very regular, making atrial fibrillation unlikely.

 Ventricular Tachycardia (VT)

  • VT typically presents with:

    • Wide QRS complexes
    • AV dissociation
    • Often with capture/fusion beats
  • This ECG shows narrow QRS complexes, so it is not VT.

Sinus Tachycardia

  • Sinus tachycardia shows:

    • Normal P waves before every QRS
    • Gradual increase in heart rate
    • Rates usually <150 bpm
  • In this ECG:
    • P waves are not clearly visible
    • Heart rate is too fast for sinus tachycardia
  • Thus, sinus tachycardia is ruled out.

Summary:

The narrow complex, rapid, regular tachycardia without visible P waves makes SVT (specifically AVNRT or AVRT) the most likely diagnosis.

choices.title: Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) Syndrome
choices.correct_explanation:
The changes seen in ECG of WW syndrome are:

  • Short PR interval (<120 ms)
  • Slurring and slow rise of initial upstroke of QRS complex known as Delta waves
  • Wide QRS complex (>0.12 sec)

Wolff Parkinson White Syndrome (WPW) is characterized by an abnormal accessory pathway in the heart leading to arrhythmias.

Pathology- Born with an accessory pathway, the bundle of Kent which connects the atria and ventricle. The electrical impulses from the SA node reach the ventricles earlier via the accessory pathway as there is no AV nodal delay in this pathway. This leads to the pre-excitation of the ventricle and initiation of ventricular contraction. This ventricular contraction is prolonged when the impulse via the AV nodal pathway reaches the ventricles.

Most common location of the accessory pathway- between the left atrium and free wall of the left ventricle

ECG changes:

  • Shortened PR interval- because of the early initiation of ventricular depolarization
  • Prolonged QRS duration- because of the AV nodal impulse reaching the ventricles after the aberrant impulse
  • Delta waves- slurred upstroke of QRS complex

The given ECG shows delta waves marked with red arrows:

Treatment:  

  • Catheter ablation is the treatment of choice.
  • Anti-arrhythmic drugs like procainamide, amiodarone, quinidine, propafenone, dofetilide are used in slowing conduction in the accessory pathway (prolong refractory period).        
  • IV procainamide is the drug of choice in a hemodynamically stable WPW presenting with atrial fibrillation.
  • DC cardioversion is done in hemodynamically unstable patients.

• CXR is the initial examination of choice.

Four classical findings are:-

  • Visceral pleural lines: As air collects in the pleural space it separates the parietal and visceral pleura, with the latter being pushed inwards. Thus there is air density lining the visceral pleura (water density) –this gives rise to a sharp margin of the visceral pleura becoming visible-DEDS/Silhouette sign. 
  • Hyperlucency with absent vascular marking: The pleural space filled with air appearance hyperlucent (excessive black) with absent vascular marking-as there are no blood vessels in the pleural space.
  • Mediastinal shift: Pleural air causes mass effect and results in mediastinal shift that is always towards the opposite side.

  • Deep sulcus sign: Mass effect may also be exerted on the ipsilateral dome of diaphragm which is pushed down and hence the CP angle sulcus appears deep down.

  • Most important complication of pneumothorax.
  • Of the above 4 classical imaging findings, if the last 2 findings are prominently seen, then Tension pneumothorax should be considered.
  • Mediastinal shift: Towards contralateral side is greater in inspiration-is diagnostic.

  • Deep sulcus sign: As result of diaphragm depression. Sometimes the dome of diaphragm may be inverted.

choices.title: Confounding variable
choices.correct_explanation:
• A confounding variable is a variable that influences both the supposed cause (independent variable) and the supposed effect (dependent variable), creating a false impression of a relationship between the two. Confounding variables can lead to biased results or incorrect conclusions about causal relationships.
    • Confounding variables can distort the apparent association between the independent and dependent variables. This occurs because the confounder is related to both the independent and dependent variables but is not part of the causal pathway.
    • For example, in a study investigating the relationship between exercise (independent variable) and weight loss (dependent variable), diet could be a confounding variable, as it may influence both the amount of exercise someone does and the degree of weight loss

Distractor Analysis:

Option

Why Incorrect

a. Independent variable

The independent variable is the variable that is manipulated or categorized to observe its effect on the dependent variable. It is the presumed cause, not a variable that affects both the cause and effect.

b. Dependent variable

The dependent variable is the outcome or effect that is being measured or observed in response to changes in the independent variable. It does not influence both the cause and effect.

c. Extraneous variable

An extraneous variable is any variable that is not intentionally studied but could affect the dependent variable. While it may interfere with the experiment, it is not necessarily linked to both the independent and dependent variables in the way a confounding variable is. An extraneous variable becomes a confounding variable if it is related to both the independent and dependent variables.

Key Related Concepts:

  • Confounding in research: Confounding occurs when an extraneous variable correlates with both the independent and dependent variables, which can mislead researchers into thinking that there is a direct relationship between the cause and effect when one does not exist.
  • Control of confounding variables: Researchers control for confounding variables through various methods, such as randomization, matching, statistical control, or designing studies that minimize their influence

Clinically Relevant Notes

  • Nursing implications: In clinical research, identifying and controlling confounding variables is crucial for drawing valid conclusions from studies that aim to establish causal relationships, such as in drug efficacy trials or epidemiological research.
  • Patient safety and research integrity: For clinical trials, ensuring that confounding variables are accounted for helps maintain the integrity of findings and ensures that any interventions or treatments shown to be effective are genuinely due to the treatment, not due to confounding factors
